overview: Blackpearl Group is a Wellington, NZ-headquartered, NZX (and now dual-listed ASX) micro-cap that builds and acquires AI-driven, data-led sales and marketing tools for US small-and-medium businesses. Its portfolio spans Pearl Diver (website-visitor identity resolution / lead intelligence), B2B Rocket (AI outbound sales agents, acquired August 2025), Bebop (an AI sales-intelligence product launched in 90 days), New Old Stamp (email-signature marketing, acquired 2023) and a newer Data-as-a-Service (DaaS) offering that embeds the group's proprietary 'Pearl Engine' dataset directly into customer revenue operations. Revenue is almost entirely US-dollar-denominated SMB spend, reported in NZD, funded to date by repeated equity raises rather than internally generated cash.

business_model.summary: Blackpearl sells subscription access to AI/data products (SaaS) and, increasingly, direct embedded data feeds (DaaS) to US SMBs and mid-market go-to-market teams. FY26 (year to 31 Mar 2026) subscription revenue was $13.7m (+77% YoY) against exit ARR of $26.8m (+114% YoY) - a roughly 2x gap between what has been contracted and what has been recognised, which management attributes to ramp-pricing on new DaaS contracts (customers phase up to full billing over ~90 days) and only a partial-year (40 days in H1) contribution from the newly acquired B2B Rocket. Growth in FY26 was overwhelmingly funded by two equity raises totalling ~$26.9m (a $15m raise in Aug-2025 at $0.95/share and a further $11.8m private placement) plus a $5m/$5.27m BNZ debt facility - not by operating cash flow, which remains deeply negative.

revenue_streams.name: SaaS subscriptions (Pearl Diver, Bebop, New Old Stamp, B2B Rocket)
revenue_streams.trend: growing but decelerating share as DaaS scales; SaaS churn 4.9% FY26, ticked back up to 5.2% in Q1 FY27

revenue_streams.name: DaaS (embedded data feeds, 'wholesale')
revenue_streams.trend: growing fast (~40% of revenue mix by Q1 FY27); FY26 churn reported as 0%, but Q1 FY27 saw a customer churn (~NZ$20k/month ARR) and the base of contracts is still small ($300k-$700k ARR each)

business_model.customer_type: B2B, weighted to US SMBs and mid-market sales/marketing teams; top-10 customers were 17% of revenue in FY25 (moderate, not extreme, concentration at the top, but each DaaS deal individually is large relative to total ARR)
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly United States end-customers; company headquartered and listed in New Zealand (NZX primary, ASX dual-listed from 2025), reports in NZD

main_competitors: generalist LLM/agent platforms (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) increasingly used to build in-house lead-gen workflows
competitive_position.market_position: Small, sub-scale challenger in a crowded and well-funded B2B data/lead-intelligence category. ARR of $26.8-27.2m is a rounding error next to ZoomInfo (~$1.2bn revenue) and well-funded private players like Clay and Apollo.io. Blackpearl's own investor materials concede this scale gap and lean on a self-commissioned 'Proto-GTM Bench' benchmark (not independently verified/audited) claiming the 'Pearl Engine' produces 25x more 'A-grade' commercial records per dollar than 'leading frontier AI models' on go-to-market tasks - a marketing claim, not a peer-reviewed or third-party-audited result, and one every competitor could contest with its own commissioned benchmark.

moat_factors.description: Management's central pitch is a data flywheel: 21-31bn signals/day and tens of thousands of campaigns train a domain-specific model that outperforms generalist LLMs on lead quality. This is plausible in principle (narrow, outcome-trained models can beat generalists on narrow tasks) but the evidence offered (a company-commissioned, 'preliminary' benchmark against just two unnamed LLMs) is not independently verifiable, and the underlying data advantage is small in absolute terms next to ZoomInfo's decades of contributor network data or Clay's waterfall-enrichment aggregation across dozens of third-party sources.

moat_factors.strength: moderate for existing DaaS clients, unproven at scale
moat_factors.description: DaaS clients embed Blackpearl's data directly into revenue workflows, which management argues raises switching costs and explains 0% FY26 churn. But DaaS is new (inception in H2 FY25) and the contract base is small ($300k-$700k ARR per client implies roughly 15-30 total DaaS contracts for ~$10m of DaaS ARR) - a 'zero churn' claim over 1-2 years with a handful of contracts is not yet statistically meaningful, and the first churn event (Q1 FY27, ~NZ$20k/month) already appeared once the base grew.

Blackpearl and its sub-brands (Pearl Diver, Bebop, B2B Rocket) have limited category recognition versus ZoomInfo or Apollo.io, which dominate SEO, review sites (G2) and enterprise procurement shortlists.

Positioned as materially cheaper than ZoomInfo/Apollo/Kaspr for SMBs, which is a genuine wedge into the price-sensitive SMB segment, but commoditisation pressure from LLM-native tools (Clay, Common Room, and generic agent frameworks that SMBs can now assemble themselves) is compressing this advantage from the low end.

No meaningful regulatory moat; data-privacy compliance (fair use of scraped/enriched contact data, CAN-SPAM, GDPR/CCPA-adjacent rules) is a shared cost of doing business across the category, not a Blackpearl-specific advantage.

weaknesses: Sub-scale versus well-capitalised, VC-backed or public competitors (ZoomInfo, Apollo.io, Clay) with far larger data assets and marketing budgets
Core moat claim rests on a single, preliminary, company-commissioned benchmark rather than independent verification
DaaS 'zero churn' track record is short (about 18 months) and built on a small number of large contracts, making it highly sensitive to a single logo loss - which has already begun (Q1 FY27 churn)
Product line is an assembled portfolio of small/bolt-on acquisitions (New Old Stamp, B2B Rocket) rather than one deeply integrated platform, raising execution/integration risk

Structurally exposed to LLM commoditisation: as frontier models get cheaper and better at exactly the lead-finding/enrichment tasks Blackpearl sells, the addressable premium for a smaller vertical player narrows

growth_drivers: DaaS scale-out: management guides to DaaS becoming a larger share of the mix, with deeper embedding, higher per-contract ARR ($300k-$700k) and (they claim) structurally lower churn than SaaS

B2B Rocket cross-sell: full-year contribution (only 40 days recognised in H1 FY26) plus Pearl Engine-driven ARPU uplift post-integration; management cites $1.8m of annualised FY27 cost synergies against a $0.5m integration cost

Compressing the ARR-to-revenue timing lag: shorter DaaS ramp cycles, tighter ideal-customer-profile (ICP) targeting, and improved cash collection are explicit 'five levers' management has called out for FY27

Gross margin operating leverage: data supply agreements moved from variable to a fixed annual cost structure in FY26, so as revenue scales without a matching cost increase, gross margin should mechanically expand (69% FY26, guided higher in FY27)
Stated path to $50m ARR within 3-5 years and a $30m ARR milestone described as 'fast approaching' as of the FY26 result

Q1 FY27 already shows sequential progress: EBITDAF loss narrowing from $4.5m (Q1) toward a guided $1.0-1.5m (Q3) - if delivered, this would be the first real evidence of operating leverage translating into cash discipline

business.description: $26.8m FY26 ARR vs $13.7m recognised subscription revenue is roughly a 2x gap. Management attributes this to ramp pricing and partial-period acquisition contribution, but a persistent, widening gap between headline ARR and cash-generating revenue is exactly the metric investors should be most skeptical of in a story stock, and it directly explains part of the share-price disconnect from the ARR growth headline.

DaaS contracts run $300k-$700k in ARR each, implying roughly 15-30 total DaaS relationships underpin ~$10m+ of ARR. The heavily marketed '0% churn in FY26' claim is a small-sample, short-history statistic that has already broken (one DaaS customer churned in Q1 FY27, ~NZ$20k/month ARR). A handful of further DaaS losses would materially dent both ARR growth and the 'sticky data embedding' narrative.

financial.description: H1 FY26 alone burned $7.2m of FCF (vs $5.8m for the whole of FY24) and net free cash outflow excluding the B2B Rocket acquisition was $7.1m in just six months. Cash was $9.59m at 31 Mar 2026 against a burn rate that, annualised at the H1 pace, would exhaust cash in well under 12 months without further capital. FY26 EBITDAF loss was $15.7m (including $10.2m of one-off costs); even stripping those one-offs, run-rate losses remain large relative to the cash balance. The company has already added $5.3m of BNZ debt (refinanced to March 2028) on top of two equity raises totalling $26.9m in FY26 alone - a pattern of continuous external funding, not self-sufficiency.

Shares outstanding roughly doubled from 53.3m (FY24) to about 97m (mid-2026) - approximately 82% dilution in two years, and roughly 53% just from FY25 to H1-FY26. Both FY26 capital raises (Aug-2025 placement/entitlement offer at $0.95, and the subsequent $11.8m placement) were priced well below the Nov-2024 peak of ~$1.39 and each added meaningfully to the share count. Continued cash burn makes further dilutive raises likely unless the FY27 loss-narrowing trajectory (guided Q3 FY27 EBITDAF loss of $1.0-1.5m) is actually delivered.

$5.27m of loans/borrowings (mostly the BNZ facility, extended to March 2028) sit on a balance sheet with persistent operating losses; covenant or refinancing risk rises if losses do not narrow as guided.
Revenue is overwhelmingly USD-denominated (US SMB customers) while the company reports in NZD and is NZX/ASX-listed; NZD/USD and AUD/NZD moves create translation noise in reported growth rates.

regulatory.description: The core product is built on scraped/enriched B2B contact and behavioural data; tightening US state privacy laws, CAN-SPAM-style enforcement, or platform-level restrictions (e.g., LinkedIn/email providers clamping down on outbound automation and enrichment) could raise compliance costs or restrict data sourcing for Pearl Diver, B2B Rocket and DaaS alike.
ASX dual-listing (2025) adds ongoing compliance and reporting costs; $1.2m of FY26's one-off costs were directly attributed to ASX listing and associated expenses.

macro.description: Customer base is US SMBs, a discretionary-spend cohort that is typically first to cut software/marketing spend in a slowdown; CAC payback already lengthened from 3.5 to 6.3 months into Q1 FY27, which management frames as a deliberate trade but could equally reflect softening SMB demand or tougher new-logo economics.

Market cap in the tens of millions of NZD with thin daily turnover (August 2026 trading: ~72k shares, ~$31k value in a single day). Small-cap, loss-making, story-stock names are typically the first sold in a risk-off environment, and illiquidity itself widens the range of plausible fair prices - amplifying both the 2024 run-up to $1.39 and the subsequent collapse to $0.43.

macro.risk: LLM commoditisation of the core product category
macro.description: General-purpose LLMs and agent frameworks are rapidly improving at exactly the lead-finding/enrichment/outreach tasks Blackpearl monetises. If frontier models close even part of the quality gap Blackpearl's own benchmark claims, the pricing premium and differentiation for a small vertical player erodes quickly - a structural threat larger, better-capitalised competitors (ZoomInfo, Apollo, Clay) are also racing to address, but from a position of far greater data scale and R&D budget.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: B2B sales intelligence / data-as-a-service is a large, growing category (driven by AI-enabled outbound and account-based marketing) but is also rapidly commoditising as LLMs absorb enrichment and lead-scoring workflows that used to require dedicated vendors. Growth is real across the sector, but competitive intensity and price pressure are both rising simultaneously.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - reliant on US SMB marketing/sales tooling budgets, which are among the more discretionary and cyclical categories of software spend.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High indirectly: as an unprofitable, cash-burning micro-cap reliant on repeated equity/debt raises to fund growth, higher rates and risk-off conditions directly raise its cost/availability of capital and depress the multiple the market will pay for ARR growth.
key_input_costs: Third-party/underlying data supply agreements (now fixed-cost annual contracts)
Cloud/compute costs for the Pearl Engine and LLM-adjacent infrastructure
US sales & marketing headcount (SMB go-to-market is labour- and CAC-intensive)

recent_developments.event: Announced acquisition of US-based B2B Rocket Inc. (AI outbound sales automation, ~US$2.1m ARR at acquisition) and intention to dual-list on the ASX

Completed B2B Rocket acquisition (21 Aug 2025) for US$4m cash plus 1.725m BPG shares; launched a $15m capital raise ($7m institutional placement + ~$8m accelerated entitlement offer) at a fixed price of NZ$0.95/share, a 13.6% discount to the prior close

H1 FY26 result: ARR $19.5m (+87% YoY), subscription revenue $5.15m, net loss $7.34m, net free cash outflow $7.1m (ex B2B Rocket acquisition), gross margin compressed to 67% (crossover between variable and fixed data-supply agreements)
Completed a further $11.8m private placement, broadening the institutional shareholder base (including new Australian institutions) to fund product expansion and platform development

FY26 (year to 31 Mar 2026) full-year result: record ARR $26.8m (+114% YoY), subscription revenue $13.7m (+77% YoY), gross margin 69%, EBITDAF loss $15.7m (including $10.2m of one-off acquisition/listing/offer costs), cash $9.6m, BNZ facility refinanced to $5m/March 2028; management flagged a 'five levers' plan to compress the ARR-to-revenue timing lag and prioritise cash conversion in FY27

Q1 FY27 trading update: ARR $27.2m (+95% YoY, +2% sequential), EBITDAF loss $4.5m, guidance for losses to narrow to $2.5-3.0m (Q2 FY27) and $1.0-1.5m (Q3 FY27); SaaS churn ticked up to 5.2%; CAC payback lengthened to 6.3 months (from 3.5 months); DaaS now ~40% of revenue mix but recorded its first customer churn (~NZ$20k/month ARR)

Shares trading around NZ$0.43 (7-8 Aug 2026), down roughly 69% from the Nov-2024 peak of ~$1.39 and roughly 43% YTD in 2026, despite record ARR growth - reflecting market skepticism on cash burn, dilution, ARR-to-revenue conversion lag, and DaaS concentration rather than any single negative catalyst identified in company announcements to date

guidance.as_of: Q1 FY27 trading update (~June/July 2026) and FY26 results (May 2026)

items.vs_prior: new - implies ~70% sequential loss narrowing from Q1 FY27's $4.5m loss to the Q3 midpoint
items.notes: First quantified path to breakeven; delivery is the key swing factor for whether further dilutive capital raises are needed
Company describes the $30m ARR milestone as 'fast approaching, ahead of internal expectations' as of the FY26 result (ARR was $26.8m at FY26-end, $27.2m at Q1 FY27)
Driven mechanically by the fixed (vs previously variable) data-supply-agreement cost structure as revenue scales

items.target: Elevated to an equal-weighted priority alongside ARR growth
items.vs_prior: new emphasis - a shift from FY26's growth-at-all-costs framing
items.notes: Explicit acknowledgement that FY26/FY27 strategy must now demonstrate it can convert ARR into cash, not just growth

guidance.management_commentary: FY26 result commentary: 'The $10.2 million in one-off non-recurring costs in FY26 are now behind us... Five specific levers are now in motion - each directly converting contracted ARR into recognised revenue and cash' (shorter ramp cycles, tighter customer profiles, post-acquisition cost optimisation, improved cash collection, fixed-cost infrastructure leverage). Q1 FY27 update frames the lengthened CAC payback (3.5 to 6.3 months) as 'a deliberate trade for transition' rather than a demand-side weakening, and reiterates DaaS as 'validated as a zero-churn, compounding revenue stream' despite the first DaaS churn event occurring in the same quarter.

bull_case: FY26 ARR growth of 114% YoY and Q1 FY27 ARR of $27.2m (+95% YoY) is genuinely rapid top-line momentum, and if the guided Q1-to-Q3 FY27 EBITDAF loss narrowing (roughly $4.5m to $1.0-1.5m) is delivered, the business could reach breakeven without further heavily dilutive raises
Gross margin structurally improving (67% to 69%, guided higher) as data-supply costs shift from variable to fixed - a genuine operating-leverage mechanism, not just a promise

DaaS is a real product innovation for the category - embedding data directly into a customer's revenue workflow plausibly does raise switching costs versus a standalone SaaS seat, and even a moderated (non-zero) churn rate could make DaaS a materially better business than pure SaaS lead-gen tools
The ~69% collapse in share price since Nov-2024 already discounts significant execution risk; if FY27 guidance is met, the stock is starting from a low valuation base relative to $26.8m+ of ARR

B2B Rocket's full-year contribution (only 40 days recognised in H1 FY26) has not yet flowed through the P&L, so FY27 subscription revenue should mechanically catch up toward the ARR run-rate even without further sales execution
bear_case: Share count has grown from 53.3m to roughly 97m in about two years (~82% dilution), funded by successive equity raises priced below prior peaks, and the FY26 cash burn ($15.7m EBITDAF loss, $7m+ H1 free cash outflow alone) makes further dilution likely unless the FY27 loss-narrowing guidance is met precisely

The ~2x gap between $26.8m ARR and $13.7m recognised revenue is not fully explained by ramp timing alone and deserves scrutiny as a metric-quality issue; ARR is a forward-looking, non-audited KPI that the company itself controls the definition of, while recognised revenue is the audited, cash-relevant number

The headline '0% DaaS churn' claim, built on a small number ($300k-$700k ARR each) of contracts over an ~18-month history, already broke in Q1 FY27 with the first DaaS customer loss - undermining the core 'sticky, self-reinforcing' investment thesis management has built around DaaS

The claimed moat (a 25x-better proprietary 'Pearl Engine') rests on a single, preliminary, company-commissioned benchmark against unnamed competitor models, not independent verification, in a category (B2B contact data/lead intelligence) dominated by far larger, better-capitalised incumbents (ZoomInfo, Apollo.io) and fast-moving, well-funded challengers (Clay, Common Room) - all of whom face the same LLM-commoditisation pressure Blackpearl does, but from a stronger data and capital position

NZX/ASX micro-cap illiquidity (tens of thousands of dollars of daily turnover) means the stock can re-rate sharply on thin volume in either direction, and a loss-making, dilution-dependent story stock is typically among the first sold in a risk-off market - which is a more parsimonious explanation for the -69% peak-to-trough move than any single fundamental catalyst identified in company disclosures to date
